title: Mr. Market Got Generous With My September Pick, So I Added
description: A regulatory penalty, a soft quarter and a 40bp jump in rates. I cut fair value, kept the BUY and took the weight to 5%.
body_html:
Maybe I shouldn’t admit this… but here goes.

I hate banks.

I don’t mean I hate them as an investment; you’ve seen that I always have banks in the portfolio. In fact, I invest in them for the very reason I hate them.

Let me explain.

I bet most of you have had this happen when checking your monthly statement (if you don’t check yours, I suggest you do). Back when I was a student, I noticed a fee on my FREE student account. It was only $4.95, but I was so pissed that I called the bank. After a long wait and a maze of phone menus, I reached an agent who explained the charge came from some fine print. That was CIBC. A year later, the same thing happened with TD, and I still get those surprises every now and then.

There’s a reason people don’t like banks. Only 28% of Americans have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in them.

Then came the 2008 financial crisis, caused partly by banks selling products to people who didn’t qualify for them. They didn’t even get a slap on the wrist. They got government help and paid themselves ridiculous bonuses.

We’ve seen this happen several times, and I bet we’ll see it again.

The reason they get away with it is simple… they’re too big to fail.

That’s why we’ve seen banks fined billions, and they still survive and thrive. My point is that the $1.2B fine on BAC isn’t a game changer. It’s part of the business, and sadly, BAC will thrive.

Four weeks ago I made a BAC my September pick. The argument was that Mr. Market was using the wrong discount rate, and that the company’s own capital structure showed it.

This week the bank took three hits in two days: a regulatory penalty, a soft quarter and another leg up in bond yields. The stock had a rough two days. This morning I bought more.

Table of Contents

  • TLDR

  • The penalty, and what eleven precedents say about it

  • Q3 2026 results

  • Guidance: what changed

  • The rate the thesis depends on

  • Thesis scorecard after Q3 2026

  • Valuation: what moved the target

  • Risk register

  • Performance vs. peers

  • Verdict

Mr. Market handed me a cheaper entry yesterday and I took it.

Since I added Bank of America [] to the portfolio on 15 September, the stock is down 14%.

In the September deep dive, my opening exhibit was an afternoon when Mr. Market took $23B off this bank for $300M of investment banking fees. The argument was that the market had stopped examining the one number that moves the valuation most: the rate it uses to discount BAC’s future profits.

This week Mr. Market ran the same experiment with a bigger prompt. Earlier this week, the Treasury announced $1.2B of anti-money laundering and sanctions penalties against BAC. Yesterday, BAC reported a third quarter with soft trading, expenses growing faster than revenue and a 2% revenue miss. The stock opened down 8% and was trading at $51 by lunch. Two days, $24B of market value.

Then September CPI came in at 3.7% vs. 3.6% expected and pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 5.3% intraday before easing back to 5.2%.

For my thesis, that third headline matters more than the other two combined, because the risk-free rate is the first input into the discount rate the whole September argument was about.

I added at $50.08 this morning, taking BAC from 3.36% to 5% of the portfolio.

I funded the add with a little margin. The market is in the red today, so I’m going slightly into margin (1.7%) to cover the gap and will sell something on a green day. I’m also cutting my fair value for BAC.

TLDR

  • The penalty is $1.2B, 4% of a year’s earnings and 0.3% of market value. No asset cap, no monitor, no criminal case. In the precedents with terms like these, the share-price damage was gone within weeks.

  • Q3 revenue grew 3% y/y and missed consensus by 2%. EPS excluding the charge was in line. NII +8%, wealth management revenue +13%, FICC -17%.

  • Operating leverage turned negative. Adjusted expenses grew 7% while revenue grew 3%. This is the pillar I’m marking down.

  • The 10-year is up 40bp since I built the model. The two preferreds I highlighted in September repriced 30bp-34bp. The return Mr. Market demands on the common rose 110bp.

  • Fair value goes from $83 to $72, and BAC stays a BUY. Upside is +41%, vs. +39% at the pick.

  • I added: BAC goes from 3.36% to 5% of the portfolio.

The penalty, and what eleven precedents say about it

What BAC agreed to. Yesterday, the Treasury announced penalties of $1.21B. FinCEN fined BAC $1.2B and credited the OCC’s $750M civil money penalty inside that figure, the largest penalty the OCC has ever imposed. OFAC added $11.6M for 475 apparent sanctions violations across the Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and terrorism programmes, and classed them as non-egregious.

BAC admitted willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. In the FinCEN consent order, willful is the civil standard, which means reckless disregard rather than knowing intent. The conduct runs from January 2018 to July 2025, and a 2024 internal lookback found 8,900 suspicious activity reports that should have been filed, covering $4B of transactions.

What’s missing from the orders matters more. Nothing caps BAC’s balance sheet, restricts its growth, installs a monitor or limits dividends and buybacks, and no DOJ case has been reported. The required work is a third-party lookback plus independent reviews of transaction monitoring, customer due diligence, correspondent banking and data governance, focused on the southwest border, Iran and Russia. BAC says the remediation spend, a couple of hundred million dollars a quarter plus thousands of staff, already sits in the expense run rate, and it bought back $6B of stock in Q3 anyway.

The arithmetic. The charge isn’t tax-deductible and costs $0.17 a share, which is 4% of BAC’s 2025 net income and 0.4% of book. Mr. Market took $24B off over the two days, and the timing shows how much of it was the penalty. Treasury published and BAC fell 2% in after-hours trading on the penalty alone. On Wednesday, with the earnings out, BAC fell 5% while KBE [] fell 1% and JPMorgan [] rose 1%. It looks like the penalty accounts for 2 of the 6 points BAC lost this week; the quarter accounts for most of the rest.

What history says. Claude pulled for me every large bank enforcement case since 2012 with a clean share-price record, and measured each stock on the day, a month later and a year later against its own bank index.

The cases split into two groups, and the size of the cheque doesn’t decide which group a bank lands in.

The first group paid and moved on. JPM’s $2.05B Madoff settlement, HSBC’s $1.92B cartel and sanctions case, US Bancorp’s [] $613M, Standard Chartered’s 2019 $1.1B and American Express’s [] $350M last week all moved less than 2% on the day and left nothing durable a year later. BNP Paribas is the extreme test: an $8.97B guilty plea, more than a full year of profit, and the shares rose on the day because the pain had already happened in the months the number was leaking.

The second group had limits put on the business, and those limits are what cost shareholders money. The Fed’s asset cap on Wells Fargo [] came with no fine at all, and over the seven years until it was lifted, WFC returned +45% while JPM returned +186% and BAC +66%. TD Bank [] pleaded guilty and got a $434B cap on its US retail bank, and fell 10% in two days. Standard Chartered’s 2012 crash came from New York threatening its licence, which can switch off dollar clearing. Danske Bank spent four years with unquantified criminal exposure, a departed CEO and no dividend before its $2B plea, and then rallied +21pp vs. European banks in the year after the plea.

Two more patterns sit in the table. Resolution tends to be a positive catalyst: BNP, Danske and Standard Chartered 2019 all traded better once the number was known. And the expensive cases took time to recognize. TD’s underperformance was mostly priced before the plea, and Citigroup [] never had a cap, but its 2020 consent orders required OCC sign-off on acquisitions and turned into a three-year slide of 20pp against KBE.

Where BAC fits. On the terms, BAC sits in the first group. The path to watch is the one C took, because the December 2024 cease-and-desist that started this is still open, Treasury says the breakdowns continued after it, and a third-party lookback is designed to find things. If the OCC amends the order to require approval for acquisitions or to restrict growth, BAC moves into the second group and I’d revisit the thesis. Until then, the penalty is a one-quarter cost and a reputational bruise.

Q3 2026 results

GAAP EPS fell 13% y/y. Excluding the charge, EPS rose 4% and landed in line with consensus. Revenue grew 3% y/y and missed consensus by 2%. The Street had already cut, with consensus EPS sliding from $1.16 on 1 October to $1.10 at the print, so a soft capital markets quarter was expected and it still came in below.

NII carried the quarter. NII grew 8% y/y and $450M from Q2, and net interest yield excluding Global Markets rose 8bp in the quarter. Loans grew for the tenth straight quarter, up $34B in Q3, and BAC funded them by letting the held-to-maturity book run down from $506B to $496B. The deposit rate rose 3bp in a quarter when the Fed hiked, which tells you how sticky the funding base is. This is the repricing engine from the deep dive, working with rates going up instead of down.

Wealth management is the fee franchise I argued for. Revenue grew 13% and net income 22%, with a 29% pretax margin and a 28% return on allocated capital. Client balances passed $5T for the first time and AUM flows reached $74B over twelve months. These fees are a percentage of client assets, so they reprice with markets rather than with the deal calendar.

Capital markets gave back Q2. Sales and trading fell from $7.1B in Q2 to $5.1B, and 5% y/y. FICC dropped 17% because BAC’s biggest franchises are in mortgages, municipals and credit, and clients in those markets stopped trading when long rates jumped during the quarter. Equities had a record Q3. Investment banking fees fell 11% y/y and landed at the top of the $1.6B-$1.8B range the CEO gave in September, the guide that started the $23B afternoon. Year to date, investment banking fees are still +16%.

Expenses were the real miss. Adjusted expenses grew 7% y/y while revenue grew 3%, so the adjusted efficiency ratio rose to 62% from 59% in Q2. BAC’s own breakdown of the $1.2B increase: $450M of wealth incentives that follow revenue, $300M of equities brokerage and clearing costs that follow volume, and a couple of hundred million dollars for two remediation programmes, one of them the AML work. The remaining core expense growth was $200M-$300M on a $17B base, with headcount down 3,000 y/y. The revenue-linked costs will fall with revenue if markets stay quiet. The remediation spend is the part that has to come down for the operating leverage story to work.

Credit improved again. The net charge-off ratio fell to 0.44% from 0.47%, the card loss rate improved to 3.22%, card delinquencies improved y/y for the sixth straight quarter, and commercial reservable criticized exposure fell 24% y/y to its lowest level since 2019. BAC released $80M of reserves.

Guidance: what changed

The NII line is the one that moved. The 2027 guide of 8% or more sits above the 5%-7% medium-term range from Investor Day, and BAC says it includes a drag from Global Markets, whose balance sheet is liability-sensitive and earns less as rates rise. Ex-markets, the core banking book grows faster than 8%. The guide assumes three more 25bp Fed hikes, in December, March and June, on top of the one already delivered, and the rate table shows why BAC is comfortable with that: a 100bp rise is now worth more than it was in Q2, and a 100bp fall costs less.

The operating leverage line held in words and weakened in substance. BAC expects positive operating leverage again in Q4 and keeps 200bp-300bp for 2027, saying it “could be higher.” It no longer talks about the 300bp-400bp pace my deep dive leaned on.

Management credibility. On NII, BAC has under-promised: it raised the FY2026 guide twice this year, from 5%-7% to 7% and then 8%, and reaffirmed it this quarter. On markets and costs, it over-promised: the September guide called trading flat and it came in -5%, and operating leverage went negative after a strong first half. I take the NII guide at face value and haircut the operating leverage guide, which is how I’ve set the model.

The rate the thesis depends on

My September cost of equity was 8.4%: a 4.80% risk-free rate plus a beta of 0.86 times an equity risk premium of 4.23%. Since I built the model, the 10-year has gone to 5.2%, after touching 5.3% intraday on this morning’s CPI. Keep the beta and the premium where they were and the cost of equity becomes 8.8%. That one input, with nothing else touched, takes fair value from $83 to $76.

Higher rates cut both ways for this bank. They help the spread business, which is why the 2027 NII guide went up. They hurt the trading desks that live on mortgage, muni and credit flow, they knocked $1.8B off CET1 through unrealized losses on securities in Q3, and they raise the bar every future dollar of profit has to clear. My model captures the bar immediately and gives the spread benefit no credit, because I haven’t raised the ROE assumption.

The more interesting evidence is one rung up the capital structure. In September, the two low-coupon preferreds I highlighted, Series NN and QQ, yielded 6.6%. Today they yield 6.90% (PRO) and 6.94% (PRQ), PRB and PRK yield 6.75% and 6.85%, and the Series L convertible (PRL) 6.10%.

That’s a 30bp-34bp move on NN and QQ, less than the 40bp the 10-year moved. In the same week as an AML penalty, the market for BAC’s junior capital is asking for a slightly smaller premium over Treasuries than it did in September.

The common went the other way. Price-to-book equals ROE minus growth, divided by cost of equity minus growth. At the pick, with a 12.7% ROE, that identity said Mr. Market was discounting at 9.3%. Today, at $51 and 1.3x book, a 12.8% ROE implies 10.4%. The gap between what BAC’s preferred holders and its common holders demand has gone from 270bp to 350bp. My 8.8% still sits 190bp-270bp above the preferreds, the same spread I argued for in September.

So the mechanism behind the thesis got stronger this month and the timing got worse. The evidence that Mr. Market overcharges BAC’s common is wider than when I bought, and the catalyst that would close it, a market willing to accept a lower required return, moved further out with a Fed that is hiking.

Thesis scorecard after Q3 2026

Pillar #1. The repricing engine: Confirmed

Original thesis: Securities bought in 2020-2021 at 1.4%-2.1% roll off and get reinvested 150bp-200bp higher for five more years, while the industry’s margins compress.

What happened since last update: Held-to-maturity securities fell $10B in Q3. Net interest yield excluding Global Markets rose 8bp to 2.65%. FY2026 NII growth of 8% was reaffirmed and FY2027 is guided at 8% or more, above the medium-term range. The core banking book grows faster than that, by BAC’s account.

Assessment: Stronger than in September. Rising rates widen the reinvestment spread, and the engine now has loan growth and non-interest-bearing deposit growth behind it as well.

Pillar #2. The fee franchise: Evolving

Original thesis: The level of fee income is structurally higher, led by wealth management fees that reprice with asset values, and I conceded that trading growth wasn’t a run rate.

What happened since last update: Wealth revenue +13%, net income +22%, AUM flows $74B over twelve months. Sales and trading fell from $7.1B to $5.1B q/q. FICC -17% y/y. Investment banking fees -11% y/y and +16% year to date.

Assessment: A split result. The wealth half did what I said it would. The markets half normalized the way the bear case said it would, and Global Markets will earn less NII in 2027 if the Fed keeps hiking.

Pillar #3. Operating leverage and AI: Challenged

Original thesis: 300bp-400bp of operating leverage for two more years takes the efficiency ratio to the low 50s and lifts the terminal return.

What happened since last update: Q3 operating leverage was negative, with adjusted expenses +7% and revenue +3%, and the adjusted efficiency ratio rose to 62%. BAC guides positive operating leverage in Q4 and 200bp-300bp for 2027. AI-driven benefits go from $250M-$300M this year to $700M next year. Headcount is down 3,000 y/y.

Assessment: The low-50s path needs 300bp or more a year, and BAC only commits to 200bp-300bp after a negative quarter. I’m marking it down, and it’s the main reason ROE comes down in the model.

Pillar #4. The cost of equity: Challenged, on timing

Original thesis: The right cost of equity is 8.4%, anchored on BAC’s own preferreds clearing at 6.0%-6.6%, while Mr. Market discounts the common at 9.3%-10.3%. Close the gap and the stock is worth $83.

What happened since last update: The 10-year rose 40bp since I built the model, and the Fed is hiking. The preferreds repriced 30bp-34bp. The required return implied for the common rose from 9.3% to 10.4%.

Assessment: The evidence moved my way while the price moved the other. The mispricing is wider and the trigger to close it is further out.

Valuation: what moved the target

Check the model here

Fair value goes from $83 to $72. Two inputs did all of the work, and I left the payout at 48% and terminal growth at 2.5%.

The cost of equity goes from 8.4% to 8.8%. The risk-free rate moves from 4.80% to 5.2%, and the beta of 0.86 and the 4.23% equity risk premium stay where they were. On its own, this takes fair value to $76.

ROE goes from 13.2% to 12.8% for ten years, and the terminal return from 12.5% to 12.1%. Q3 earned 11.1% excluding the charge, and Q2’s 12.7% had record markets revenue in it. The 12.8% assumes 2027 NII growth of 8% or more and 200bp-300bp of operating leverage lift returns back above the Q2 level. It drops the extra 40bp that depended on the efficiency ratio reaching the low 50s. On its own, this takes fair value to $79.

Together they give $72.

The two levers are close to equal in size now. Every 50bp on the cost of equity moves fair value by $6-$7 a share, and every 50bp of sustained ROE moves it by $5.

What today’s price implies. Invert the model at $51 and an 8.8% cost of equity, and Mr. Market is pricing BAC to earn 10.5%-10.8% on its equity forever. That’s below the 11.1% it earned in Q3, the quarter with the trading slump and the weakest return of the year, and before the 2027 NII step-up. Hold my 12.8% ROE instead and the price implies a 10.4% cost of equity, 350bp above BAC’s own preferreds.

Either reading asks you to believe something about this bank that its preferred market doesn’t.

What would push fair value back toward $83:

  • A lower cost of equity. The model uses 8.8%. Back at September’s 8.4% with today’s ROE, fair value is $79. That needs the 10-year to come back below 5%, or the market to accept a smaller premium over the preferreds.

  • ROE above 12.8%. At 13.3%, which needs the efficiency ratio to fall toward the mid-50s, fair value is $77.

Risk register

First, the growth is in the wrong segments: Materialized. This was the risk I ranked as the one that would cost me money. Markets revenue normalized and Q3 returned 11.1% on equity, down from 12.7% in Q2. The ROE cut in the model is my answer to it.

Second, the consumer may be turning: Faded. Card losses and delinquencies improved again, money movement is +5% y/y, and BAC sees direct deposits growing across low, middle and high income customers, with the low end picking up.

Third, the valuation sits near a decade high on book: Faded. At 1.3x book, Mr. Market has removed a good part of the premium I had to defend in September.

Fourth, the rate sensitivity is asymmetric: Faded. The asymmetry flipped. A 100bp rise is now worth +$1.4B of NII and a 100bp fall costs $1.9B, and the curve is moving up.

Fifth, the repricing schedule is described loosely: Unchanged. The deep dive used $12B-$15B a quarter of roll-off. This quarter the number on offer was $9B a quarter from mortgage payoffs alone, a different measure again. The direction is clear; a firm quarterly pace still hasn’t been given.

The allowance cushion is unchanged too. The consumer allowance is 1.66% of loans vs. 1.78% a year ago, and BAC released $80M this quarter. Fine while credit improves, and it means less room when it doesn’t.

New: regulatory escalation. The 2024 cease-and-desist is still open and the orders require a third-party lookback. The risk is an amendment like C’s in 2020, requiring OCC approval for acquisitions or limiting growth, which cost C 20pp against its peers over three years. It materializes if the lookback finds materially more unreported activity or the OCC judges the remediation late.

New: capital headroom. CET1 is 10.9% against a 10.0% requirement, after returning $8.3B in a quarter when the penalty, $34B of loan growth and higher rates all hit capital. The GSIB surcharge could lift the requirement to 10.5% on 1 January 2027, depending on final capital rules BAC expects this quarter. If it does, the $6B quarterly buyback is the first thing to give. In my model that would raise retained capital, and at a return above the cost of equity, retained capital adds value, so this risk hurts Mr. Market’s mood more than it hurts fair value.

Performance vs. peers

Every large US bank is lower since 15 September as the 10-year went from 5.0% to 5.2% and capital markets slowed, with WFC down the most and JPM the least. The sector decline is a rates story, and BAC’s extra drop is this week’s story.

Verdict

BAC stays a BUY, with fair value lowered from $83 to $72.

I added at $50.08 yesterday, taking BAC from 3.36% to 5% of the portfolio.

The penalty cost BAC $0.17 a share. The 40bp on the 10-year cost my fair value $7 a share. Mr. Market spent the week on the first number, and the second one never made a headline.

Hi George,

Just got the subscription with your channel. I am absolutely new as nee can be to stocks. I started reading articles some months ago and was following two stocks WOLF and STRL. I missed the train once, but when i fumbled across your portfolio, you had already mentioned it long back :). This is not the first time i have seen you pick the winners before most of others do.

My quick question is, when something changes in your portfolio, do we get direct msg or do i need to keep that page open 24/7?

Thanks!
